case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourline Freight Logistics (HFL) is a private limited company in the road haulage and freight distribution sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Raman, the business moves chilled and ambient goods for regional retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HFL plans to invest $720,000 in a new fleet of fuel-efficient articulated lorries and a digital dispatch system, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. HFL faces a growing driver shortage and rising vehicle defect rates that threaten its on-time delivery record.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — April 2025: HFL's fleet completed 18,600 deliveries last month with a vehicle defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.1% in the previous quarter. On-time deliveries reached 91%, while customer complaints fell from 46 to 27 a month. Average depot turnaround time is 2.8 hours. A survey of 150 retail buyers found that 72% rank on-time delivery as the top contract criterion and 60% prefer low-emission hauliers. A staff survey of 200 drivers found that 68% would welcome a fuel-economy bonus. Maintenance records show 14 of 60 vehicles overdue for safety inspection; on-the-job training on the new lorries is available, and off-the-job courses at the regional training centre cost $750 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Freight Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (October 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on HFL's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.20 to $13.97 an hour, raising the cost of depot and driving staff. (3) Diesel and vehicle-part input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while road-freight inflation is 6.3% and retail demand for chilled distribution grew 2.9%.

questions.question_text: HFL plans to fund part of its $720,000 fleet expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HFL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan for this expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit rather than the bank loan saves HFL the interest and repayment burden on part of its $720,000 expansion. With fixed costs already at $360,000 a year and a $450,000 loan commitment, keeping the $270,000 retained profit inside the business protects cash flow: no monthly instalment reduces the cash available to pay drivers and maintain the fleet. Every dollar of interest avoided supports the $6.00 contribution earned on each of the 90,000 units, helping HFL absorb the 9.6% rise in diesel and vehicle-part costs without increasing its $14.00 selling price and losing the 72% of buyers who rank on-time delivery as the key contract criterion.

Point 2: Retaining profit also preserves ownership and reduces financial risk. As a private limited company, funding $270,000 from its own earnings means no lender can impose conditions on how the new fuel-efficient lorries and digital dispatch system are operated, and founder Priya Raman keeps full control. If demand for chilled distribution disappoints, HFL is not exposed to repossession of new vehicles that a larger loan would create. It also avoids arrangement fees and collateral requirements, so the expansion can still proceed if credit conditions tighten following the base-rate rise to 5.00%, while the remaining $450,000 loan stays manageable.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HFL's expansion, costs and financing.

questions.question_text: HFL is tendering for new retail contracts. Consider national television advertising, trade magazine advertising, or social media marketing. Which should HFL choose to win new contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would build rapid brand awareness among millions of viewers and could position HFL as a low-emission haulier across the whole region. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 60-employee firm already funding a $720,000 fleet expansion, and most viewers are not commercial retail buyers, so spend would be heavily wasted. It is hard to measure whether any of the 72% of buyers who rank on-time delivery actually saw the advert.

Trade magazine advertising: Placing adverts in road-freight and retail supply publications reaches exactly the logistics managers who award contracts, at a fraction of television cost, and messages about the new fuel-efficient lorries and 91% on-time record can be backed with detail. Its weakness is narrow reach and a long lead time; magazines are monthly and may miss buyers who do not read that title, so it cannot alone fill the capacity created by the expansion.

Social media marketing: Targeted posts and short videos can demonstrate the digital dispatch system, the falling 2.4% defect rate and the fuel-economy bonus that 68% of drivers welcome, reaching buyers cheaply with measurable clicks and quick updates. Results can be slower to convert into formal tenders and require constant content, but cost per reached buyer is low.

Recommendation: HFL should choose trade magazine advertising as its main channel, supported by low-cost social media posts. It reaches the 72% of retail buyers who decide contracts on reliability, is affordable beside the $450,000 loan, and suits a technical selling proposition. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; social media alone is rejected because it cannot by itself persuade procurement teams, so it should reinforce rather than replace the trade campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal reference to HFL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to HFL and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in HFL's context with a clear, well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the rejected option lose.

questions.question_text: HFL's driver shortage and rising vehicle defect rates are worrying management. Explain two benefits for HFL of using democratic leadership to improve performance in its fleet team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HFL's 60 drivers a real voice in how the new lorries and digital dispatch system are introduced, which raises job satisfaction and helps tackle the driver shortage. Because the firm employs a workforce of 60 with a hierarchical structure, consulting drivers on route planning and shift patterns makes them feel valued and more willing to stay, reducing recruitment costs. Engaged drivers are also more likely to report faults early, so the vehicle defect rate can fall further from its current 2.4% and the 91% on-time delivery record can be protected.

Point 2: Involving drivers generates practical ideas from the people who actually operate the vehicles, improving quality and safety. Drivers who help set inspection routines can spot the maintenance issues behind the 14 vehicles overdue for inspection, cutting the risk of breakdowns that push complaints up. Higher involvement also supports the planned $750 per-driver training: consulted staff are more receptive to off-the-job courses, so the investment in skills is more effective and HFL can meet the 72% of buyers who demand reliable, on-time deliveries.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HFL's shortage, defect rate and delivery record.

questions.question_text: HFL must train drivers to operate the new fuel-efficient lorries and reduce the vehicle defect rate. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the regional training centre. Which should HFL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning on HFL's own lorries and depot is directly relevant to the new fleet and the digital dispatch system, costs no course fees, and keeps drivers productive while they learn, protecting the 91% on-time delivery rate and the 18,600 monthly deliveries. It also lets experienced drivers pass on practical fault-spotting habits that can push the 2.4% defect rate lower. The drawback is that trainers are working drivers whose own deliveries may slip, bad habits can be copied, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if retail buyers ask for proof of competence.

Off-the-job courses: The regional centre charges $750 per driver, so training the 14 overdue or newly recruited drivers would cost $10,500 (14 × $750), a small sum beside the $720,000 expansion. Courses give structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate, which supports HFL's bid for the 60% of buyers preferring low-emission hauliers. However, drivers are away from the depot, reducing short-term capacity, and generic content may not match HFL's exact vehicles, so some on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: HFL should choose on-the-job training first, with short off-the-job courses for the 14 drivers needing certification. On-the-job training is cheaper, fleet-specific and avoids losing delivery capacity while the driver shortage persists; full off-the-job training is rejected because losing drivers from the depot and spending $10,500 up front would disrupt service to the 72% of buyers who judge HFL on reliability. Staggering the $750 courses for the 14 drivers would limit lost capacity, and depot coaching would translate generic course content into the specific inspection routines needed to push the 2.4% defect rate lower and protect the 18,600 monthly deliveries.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HFL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods with reference to HFL's costs and operations.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in HFL's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HFL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $360,000 ÷ $6.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HFL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units gives a margin of safety of 30,000 units, confirming a comfortable buffer and informing whether to add more lorries to the new fleet.
2. Contribution of $6.00 a unit lets managers model price changes: a hypothetical $1.00 discount would cut contribution to $5.00 and raise break-even to $360,000 ÷ $5.00 = 72,000 units, showing the volume needed to keep the expansion viable.
3. With fixed costs of $360,000, managers can set the delivery-volume target needed to service the $450,000 loan and judge whether the 91% on-time record can be maintained before committing further capital.
4. Unit cost of $12.00 ($360,000 ÷ 90,000 units = $4.00 fixed cost per unit, plus $8.00 variable cost) can be benchmarked each quarter to track the 9.6% diesel cost rise, while labour productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,500 units per worker helps assess the driver shortage.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 30,000 units vs 90,000 output; price-discount modelling vs $360,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume target; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.00 with productivity of 1,500 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HFL's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HFL's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 revenue of $4,000,000 less cost of sales of $2,400,000 gives gross profit of $1,600,000; in 2025 revenue of $5,000,000 less $2,750,000 gives $2,250,000. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives 40.0% and 45.0%. Operating profit of $600,000 in 2024 and $900,000 in 2025, each divided by revenue, gives 15.0% and 18.0%. Dividing operating profit by capital employed of $3,000,000 and $3,600,000 gives 20.0% and 25.0%.

Evaluation: All three measures point the same way. The first margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, meaning HFL kept more of each sales dollar after direct costs despite the 9.6% rise in diesel and parts, suggesting control of variable costs or a better price mix across the 90,000 units. The overall margin improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, so overheads were absorbed more effectively as revenue grew by $1,000,000. The return on capital climbed from 20.0% to 25.0%, showing the $3,600,000 of capital employed is being used more productively; this matters because the firm is servicing a $450,000 loan and planning a $720,000 fleet expansion. Interest payable did rise from $80,000 to $100,000, but it remains small relative to operating profit, so financing costs are not yet undermining returns.

Conclusion: HFL's profitability has clearly improved. Every measure moved favourably, and the improvement is broad-based rather than a one-off, since revenue, gross profit and operating profit all rose together. The main caution is that a higher base interest rate could lift that interest charge further, so management should watch financing costs while proceeding with the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Correctly calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years with detailed evaluation of margins, capital use and interest costs and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HFL of introducing a fuel-economy bonus for its drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A fuel-economy bonus directly rewards the 68% of HFL's 200 surveyed drivers who said they would welcome one, so it can raise motivation and reduce the driver shortage by making the firm a more attractive employer. It also gives drivers a financial reason to adopt smoother driving techniques, which could lower the $8.00 variable cost per unit through reduced diesel use and help absorb the 9.6% rise in diesel and vehicle-part costs without raising the $14.00 price.

Disadvantage: The bonus adds to labour costs at a time when the national minimum wage is rising 5.8% to $13.97 an hour, squeezing the $6.00 contribution per unit. Because the insert gives no driver pay or hours, the total bonus cost cannot be reliably quantified. It may also encourage drivers to chase fuel savings at the expense of delivery speed, risking the 91% on-time record that 72% of retail buyers rank as the top contract criterion, and the scheme could create resentment if routes differ in fuel efficiency.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using HFL's survey, costs and market data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in diesel and vehicle-part costs will affect HFL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If HFL's $450,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $360,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may make future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion dearer and could dampen retail demand, but HFL can limit the damage by fixing the loan rate, so this is a manageable, one-off effect.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.97 an hour): HFL employs a workforce of 60 in which driving and depot roles are largely hourly paid, so this rise feeds directly into wage costs. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest judgement is against given productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,500 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if the driver shortage cuts output, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Input cost inflation (9.6% diesel and parts): The $8.00 variable cost per unit is affected by fuel and parts, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $8.00 = $0.77 per unit, and at 90,000 units that is about $69,000 a year (90,000 × $0.77). Even a smaller $0.50-per-unit rise would cost $45,000 a year, cutting contribution toward $5.50. HFL can recover some of this through the 60% of buyers preferring low-emission hauliers and price negotiations.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in diesel and vehicle-part costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 90,000 units, directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion, and cannot be removed by a simple fix. The interest rise is small and hedgeable, and the wage rise is significant but depends on the unstated hours and on productivity that HFL can influence, so both are smaller threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to HFL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HFL's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
